avenue.label: supported
avenue.says: Passeig de Gràcia is one of Barcelona's major avenues, running through the central Eixample from Plaça Catalunya, and holds several of the city's most celebrated buildings.
quote: is one of the major avenues in Barcelona (Catalonia, Spain) and one of its most important shopping and business areas, containing several of the city's most celebrated pieces of architecture.  It is located in the central part of Eixample, stretching from Plaça Catalunya to Carrer Gran de Gràcia.

lane.label: supported
lane.says: It was once a country lane called the Jesus Road between Barcelona and Gràcia, then a separate town; by 1827 it was 42 m wide and a place for aristocrats to show off horses and carriages.
quote: Formerly known as Camí de Jesús ("Jesus Road"), the Passeig de Gràcia was originally little more than a quasi-rural lane surrounded by gardens joining Barcelona and Gràcia, which was then still a separate town.
The new avenue was 42 metres (138 ft) wide in 1827 and became a favourite place for aristocrats to display their horse riding skills and expensive horse-drawn carriages all through the 19th century.

benches.label: supported
benches.says: In 1906 Pere Falqués designed the avenue's ornate benches and street lights.
quote: In 1906 the architect Pere Falqués i Urpí designed the avenue's now famous ornate benches and street-lights.

tiles.label: supported
tiles.says: Gaudí designed hexagonal green floor tiles with seaweed, shells and starfish for Casa Batlló; they were used in Casa Milà instead, and later chosen to pave Passeig de Gràcia.
quote: Around that time he designed hexagonal hydraulic floor tiles for Casa Batlló, they were eventually used instead for the Casa Milà; they were a green colour and were decorated with seaweed, shells and starfish. These tiles were subsequently chosen to pave Barcelona's Passeig de Gràcia.

what.label: supported
what.says: Casa Milà, popularly La Pedrera, the stone quarry, for its rough-hewn look, was the last private residence Gaudí designed, built between 1906 and 1912.
quote: popularly known as La Pedrera

"the stone quarry") in reference to its unconventional rough-hewn appearance, is a Modernista building in Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain. It was the last private residence designed by architect Antoni Gaudí and was built between 1906 and 1912.

owners.label: supported
owners.says: It was commissioned in 1906 by Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon, who planned to live on the main floor and rent out the rest.
quote: The building was commissioned in 1906 by Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon.
with the idea of living in the main floor and renting out the rest of the apartments

nickname.label: supported
nickname.says: La Pedrera was a nickname given by citizens who disapproved; the building was ridiculed in humorous publications of the time.
quote: the name "La Pedrera" is in fact a nickname assigned by the citizens who disapproved of its unusualness. The unique structure of the building and the relationship between the building's architect and Pere Milà became the object of ridicule for the people of Barcelona and many humorous publications of the time.

facade.label: supported
facade.says: The stone façade is self-supporting, free of load-bearing walls, so inner walls can be moved without affecting the building's stability.
quote: Casa Milà is characterized by its self-supporting stone facade, meaning that it is free of load-bearing walls.
so that internal walls can be added and demolished without affecting the stability of the building

mountain.label: disputed
mountain.says: La Pedrera was inspired by a mountain, but there is no agreement about which one.
quote: Gaudí's La Pedrera was inspired by a mountain, but there is no agreement as to which mountain was the reference model.

snow.label: supported
snow.says: The upper level is covered in white tiles, evoking a snowy mountain.
quote: apart from the upper level, which is covered in white tiles, evoking a snowy mountain

rosary.label: supported
rosary.says: Gaudí meant it as a spiritual symbol: an excerpt from the Rosary runs along the cornice, and statues of Our Lady of the Rosary with the archangels Michael and Gabriel were planned.
quote: Gaudí, a Catholic and a devotee of the Virgin Mary, planned for the Casa Milà to be a spiritual symbol. Overt religious elements include an excerpt from the Rosary on the cornice and planned statues of Mary, specifically Our Lady of the Rosary, and two archangels, St. Michael and St. Gabriel.

statues-dropped.label: supported
statues-dropped.says: After the Tragic Week, an outbreak of anticlericalism, Milà dropped the religious statues; Gaudí thought of abandoning the project, but a priest persuaded him to continue.
quote: After Semana Trágica, an outbreak of anticlericalism in the city, Milà prudently decided to forgo the religious statues. Gaudí contemplated abandoning the project but a priest persuaded him to continue.

ironwork.label: supported
ironwork.says: The twisting wrought-iron balconies were controversial at the time.
quote: it was controversial because of its undulating stone facade, twisting wrought iron balconies

courtyards.label: supported
courtyards.says: The building is arranged around two courtyards that bring light to all nine levels; instead of a dark lobby, the open courtyards are visible as you enter.
quote: Casa Milà consists of two buildings, which are structured around two courtyards that provide light to the nine stories
Its open and airy courtyards provide a place of transit and are directly visible to those accessing the building.

lifts.label: tradition
lifts.says: Gaudí wanted the residents to know each other, so lifts stopped only on every other floor.
quote: Gaudí wanted the people who lived in the flats to all know each other. Therefore, there were only elevators on every other floor, so people on different floors would meet one another.

garage.label: supported
garage.says: The basement was a garage for cars, then a new invention; Gaudí removed a pillar on the ramp so a neighbor's Rolls-Royce could get in.
quote: During construction there was a problem including a basement as a garage for cars, the new invention that was thrilling the bourgeois at the time.
requested a change because his Rolls-Royce could not access it. Gaudí agreed to remove a pillar on the ramp that led into the garage

violin.label: tradition
violin.says: Roser Segimon complained there was no straight wall for her Steinway piano; Gaudí answered, "So play the violin."
quote: This was another point of friction with Segimon, who complained that there was no straight wall to place her Steinway piano. Gaudí's response was blunt: "So play the violin."

attic.label: supported
attic.says: The attic, once the laundry, sits under 270 brick arches spaced about 80 cm apart, like the ribs of a huge animal.
quote: The attic, where the laundry rooms were located, was a clear room under a Catalan vault roof supported by 270 parabolic vaults of different heights and spaced by about 80 cm. The roof resembles both the ribs of a huge animal and a palm

chain.label: supported
chain.says: To draw each arch, the builders hung a chain against the wall and traced the curve it made.
quote: From these nails was dangled a chain so that the lowest point coincided with the deflection of the arch. Then the profile displayed on the wall by the chain was drawn

roof.label: supported
roof.says: The roof has six skylights and staircase exits and twenty-eight chimneys; the poet Pere Gimferrer called it the garden of warriors, because the chimneys seem to guard the skylights.
quote: On the rooftop there are six skylights/staircase exits
twenty-eight chimneys in several groupings
called "the garden of warriors" by the poet Pere Gimferrer because the chimneys appear to be protecting the skylights

helmets.label: supported
helmets.says: The chimneys are covered in ceramics, with shapes that suggest medieval helmets; the staircase towers are topped with the four-armed cross.
quote: Notable features are the staircases to the roof, topped with the four-armed cross, and the chimneys, covered in ceramics and with shapes that suggest mediaeval helmets.

bottles.label: legend
bottles.says: One chimney is topped with glass; it was said Gaudí used the empty bottles from the inauguration party. It was restored with old champagne bottle bases.
quote: One of the chimneys was topped with glass pieces – it was said that Gaudí did that the day after the inauguration of the building, taking advantage of the empty bottles from the party. It was restored with the bases of champagne bottles from the early twentieth century.

unesco.label: verified
unesco.says: UNESCO lists Casa Milà-La Pedrera among the Works of Antoni Gaudí; its roof, attics and noble floor have been comprehensively restored.
quote: The Casa Milà-La Pedrera has been comprehensively restored to improve its state of conservation, highlight certain unique features such as the roof, attics, “noble” floor, etc.

resident.label: supported
resident.says: As of 2026, one resident still lives in the building, the writer Ana Viladomiu.
quote: As of 2026, the writer Ana Viladomiu is the building's sole remaining resident.

parts.name: Passeig de Gràcia
parts.stand: Stand on the opposite side of Passeig de Gràcia, across from the wavy stone building.

paras.t: You're on Passeig de Gràcia, one of the great avenues of Barcelona, and home to some of its most famous buildings. And look down at the pavement under your feet.

Those hexagonal tiles, with seaweed, shells and starfish, are a Gaudí design. He made them for Casa Batlló, used them in the building across the street instead, and later the city chose them to pave this whole avenue.

It wasn't always grand. This was once a country lane, called the Jesus Road, between Barcelona and the separate town of Gràcia. By 1827 it was 42 meters wide, and aristocrats came here to show off their horses and carriages. Those ornate benches and street lights were designed in 1906 by Pere Falqués.

parts.name: The stone façade
parts.stand: Stay across the street and take in the whole curving façade.

paras.t: That's Casa Milà. Everybody calls it La Pedrera, the stone quarry, because of that rough, rolling stone. It was the last private house Gaudí designed, built between 1906 and 1912 for Pere Milà and his wife, Roser Segimon.

The nickname wasn't a compliment. People who disliked the building gave it, and the humorous papers of the day made fun of it. Look at the balconies. That twisted wrought iron was part of the controversy too.
Gaudí was thinking of a mountain. Which mountain? Nobody knows for sure, and people still disagree. But look up at the top level, faced in white tiles, like snow on a peak.
Here's the clever part. That stone front holds itself up. It's not a load-bearing wall at all, so the walls inside can be moved without touching the building's stability.

And look along the top edge. Gaudí, devoted to the Virgin Mary, carved words from the Rosary up there. He also planned statues of Mary with the archangels Michael and Gabriel. But after the Tragic Week, an outbreak of anti-church violence in the city, Milà dropped the statues. Gaudí nearly walked away from the job. A priest talked him into staying.

parts.name: The courtyards
parts.stand: Inside, stop in the courtyard and look straight up.

paras.t: No dark lobby here. The whole building is wrapped around two open courtyards, which pour light down through every floor.
It is said that Gaudí wanted the neighbors to know each other, so the elevators stopped only on every other floor, and people from different floors would run into each other.
Cars were a thrilling new invention, so there was a garage in the basement. When one neighbor's Rolls-Royce couldn't get down the ramp, Gaudí took a pillar out for it.
Not every owner loved living in a Gaudí. It is said that Roser Segimon complained there wasn't one straight wall for her Steinway piano. Gaudí's answer: "So play the violin."

parts.name: The attic
parts.stand: Up in the attic, stand in the long brick passage and look along the arches.

paras.t: This was the laundry. Look at the arches, 270 of them, about 80 centimeters apart. It feels like standing inside the ribs of a huge animal.
How did they get that shape? The builders hung a chain against the wall, let it sag, and traced the curve. Then they built the arch along that line.

parts.name: The roof
parts.stand: Out on the roof, find a flat spot among the chimneys.

paras.t: And here's the roof. Twenty-eight chimneys and six staircase towers. The poet Pere Gimferrer called it the garden of warriors, because the chimneys seem to stand guard.
The roof goes up and down in steps and slopes. Watch your feet, and hold on to children.
Look at the chimneys covered in tiles. Their shapes suggest medieval helmets. And the staircase towers are topped with Gaudí's four-armed cross.

Look for the chimney topped with glass. The story goes that Gaudí made it the day after the party for the building's opening, from the empty bottles. When it was restored, they used the bottoms of old champagne bottles.
UNESCO lists La Pedrera as World Heritage, and this roof and the attic have been carefully restored.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Before you head down, look out over the city from the roof terrace, keeping back from the edge.

paras.t: People laughed at this building. They called it a quarry. And still, as of 2026, one person, the writer Ana Viladomiu, calls it home. Imagine having these warriors as your neighbors.
